title: Dual Practice of Chan and Pure Land
author: Zhanran
excerpt: A Chan practitioner came to visit and asked: At the moment of death, if one has not yet illumined the mind and seen the nature (thoroughly seen the original nature), or if one has illumined the mind and seen the nature but has not yet cut off the delusions of views and thoughts, what plan can end birth and death?

inline.s: A Chan practitioner came to visit and asked: At the moment of death, if one has not yet illumined the mind and seen the nature (thoroughly seen the original nature), or if one has illumined the mind and seen the nature but has not yet cut off the delusions of views and thoughts, what plan can end birth and death?
Answer: the dual practice of Chan and Pure Land.

[The delusions of views and thoughts] The view-delusions and the thought-delusions. The view-delusions are the deluded errors of ordinary beings in their views, namely the five wrong views: the view of a self, the view of extremes, the wrong view, the view of clinging to views, and the view of clinging to precepts and rules. The thought-delusions are the deluded errors of ordinary beings in their thinking, namely the afflictions of greed, hatred, ignorance, pride, and doubt. These two kinds of delusion are the root cause by which living beings drift through the three realms and undergo birth and death in vain; cutting them off is what ends birth and death and leaves the three realms.
Question: Why practice both Chan and Pure Land?
Answer: Mazu founded the monastery
Mazu was the first to establish monasteries devoted specifically to the Chan school
—the “conglin”)
, and Baizhang established the Pure Rules (the “Essential Principles of the Monastery”). These rules were set down for the Chan practitioners of the monastery, and they begin by saying:
“A monastery flourishes when it is free of affairs,
practice is most secure when it rests on Buddha-recitation

The second line, “practice is most secure when it rests on Buddha-recitation,” means: for the sake of security, while a Chan practitioner investigates Chan he should also believe and vow, reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking birth in the Pure Land (the dual practice of Chan and Pure Land). This is because, to end birth and death through Buddha-recitation and birth in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, one need only subdue the afflictions; whereas to end birth and death through investigating Chan, one must cut off the view-delusions and thought-delusions. Compared with the latter, the former is vastly easier, and so it is the secure path. Many great masters and patriarchs practiced both Chan and Pure Land, taking the Land of Utmost Bliss as their destination—for example, Master Yongming Yanshou, Master Hanshan, and Master Chewu. National Master Bojo, author of The Essentials of Cultivating the Mind, likewise practiced both, and wrote The Essential Gateway of Buddha-Recitation. Master Yongming Yanshou wrote The Four Distinctions to advocate the dual practice. Its verses read:
With Chan but without the Pure Land, / Nine of ten will lose their way; / When the bardo realm appears before them, / In a flash they are swept away.
Without Chan but with the Pure Land, / Ten thousand practice, ten thousand go; / Once they behold Amitabha, / Why worry that awakening is slow?
With both Chan and the Pure Land, / They are like a tiger crowned with horns; / In this life a teacher of the people, / In the next, a buddha or patriarch born.
With neither Chan nor the Pure Land, / The iron bed and the brazen post; / Through ten thousand kalpas, a thousand lives, / With no refuge, and no one to lean upon at all.

[Conglin] “Conglin” (monastery) usually refers to Chan monasteries, hence it is also called the “Chan grove”; but in later times monasteries of the teaching, vinaya, and other schools also imitated the Chan system and were called conglin. [Distinctions] The discerning and selecting of principles. [The Four Distinctions] Four items of discrimination (Chan without a Pure Land, no Chan but a Pure Land, both Chan and a Pure Land, and neither Chan nor a Pure Land). [Having Chan] Illumining the mind and seeing the nature (thoroughly seeing the original nature). [Having a Pure Land] True faith and earnest vows, with Buddha-recitation single-minded and undisturbed. [Having no Chan] Not having illumined the mind and seen the nature. [Having no Pure Land] Not having achieved “true faith and earnest vows, with Buddha-recitation single-minded and undisturbed.”
Question: If merely having faith, vows, and upholding the Name counts as “having a Pure Land,” why must one require single-minded, undisturbed Buddha-recitation?

Answer: Master Ouyi (the ninth patriarch of the Pure Land school), in the Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sūtra, specifically teaches: without the wondrous practice of single-minded, undisturbed Buddha-recitation, one cannot give proof of one’s true faith or fulfill one’s earnest vows. (The original text reads:
“In practice, uphold the Name with single-mindedness, undisturbed.” “Without the wondrous practice of upholding the Name, one cannot fulfill one’s vow or give proof of one’s faith.”
) Master Chewu (the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school) says:
“Single-mindedness without distraction is the final destination of pure karma and the great gate of the Pure Land. If one has not entered this gate, one is never truly secure.”

(the Collected Posthumous Writings of Master Chewu) If one’s Buddha-recitation has not yet reached single-mindedness without distraction, how can one be called “having a Pure Land,” let alone “ten thousand practice, ten thousand go”?
The Four Distinctions are annotated as follows:
[With Chan but without the Pure Land, nine of ten lose their way; when the bardo realm appears before them, in a flash they are swept away.]

If, in investigating Chan, one illumines the mind and sees the nature but has not cut off the delusions of views and thoughts (this is the case for nine of every ten who awaken), then when the bardo state appears at the end of life, one is at once carried off by the power of karma to be reborn, wholly unable to be master of oneself. However, because the view-delusions have already been cut off through the awakening, one is no longer born in the three evil destinies (hell, hungry ghosts, and animals).

[Nine of ten lose their way] Of those who illumine the mind and see the nature, at least nine out of ten have not cut off the delusions of views and thoughts; for them, practicing Chan alone is the wrong path, because nine out of ten cannot escape the cycle of birth and death. [Cuo] Error, misstep. [The bardo state] The state of the intermediate body, that is, the state that appears at the end of life from the good and evil karma of this life and of past kalpas. The moment this state appears, in the blink of an eye, according to the most powerful of one’s good or evil karma, one goes to be reborn in a good or evil destiny, with not the slightest power to be master of oneself. [In a flash] Suddenly; rapidly.
[Without Chan but with the Pure Land, ten thousand practice, ten thousand go; once they behold Amitabha, why worry that awakening is slow?]

Although one has not yet illumined the mind and seen the nature, if one has true faith and earnest vows, with Buddha-recitation single-minded and undisturbed, one is certain to be born in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss (“ten thousand practice, ten thousand go”). Having reached the Western Land of Utmost Bliss and seen Amitabha Buddha, one becomes a buddha within a single lifetime—how could one still worry about not illumining the mind and seeing the nature?
[Ten thousand practice, ten thousand go] In the Sūtra on Amitabha Buddha Spoken by the Buddha, the Buddha says:

“If there are good men and good women who hear of Amitabha Buddha and hold fast to his name—for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days—with single-mindedness, undisturbed, then when such a person approaches the end of life, Amitabha Buddha and the host of holy beings will appear before him; and at the moment of death, with a mind that is not confused, he will attain birth in Amitabha Buddha’s Land of Utmost Bliss.”

Therefore, as long as one reaches single-minded, undisturbed Buddha-recitation, one is certain to be born in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. And as far as investigative Buddha-recitation is concerned, single-mindedness without distraction is only the most elementary requirement (see
Investigative Buddha-Recitation
), and whether one’s faculties are keen or dull, anyone can reach it through diligent practice. Hence, “ten thousand practice, ten thousand go.”
[With both Chan and the Pure Land, like a tiger crowned with horns; in this life a teacher of the people, in the next, a buddha or patriarch born.]

One who has both illumined the mind and seen the nature, and also has true faith and earnest vows with single-minded, undisturbed Buddha-recitation, is like a tiger bearing horns—of matchless might. In this life he is a teacher of the multitude, and at the end of life he is born in the highest grade of the highest rank in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, becoming a buddha within a single lifetime.
[Like a tiger crowned with horns] Master Yinguang says:
“To be like a tiger crowned with horns means that such a person, through
the dual practice of Chan and Pure Land
, possesses great wisdom, great samādhi, and great eloquence. Evil spirits and heretics, upon hearing his name, are struck with terror—like a tiger bearing horns, of unmatched might.”
(the
Dharma Words of the Shanghai Dharma Assembly for Protecting the Nation and Relieving Disasters

Single-minded, undisturbed Buddha-recitation is of two kinds: single-mindedness of phenomena and single-mindedness of principle. When one who has illumined the mind and seen the nature (“having Chan”) recites the Buddha’s name, this is single-mindedness of principle, and birth in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss is in the highest grade of the highest rank; that he becomes a teacher and a buddha is only natural. On the single-mindedness of phenomena and the single-mindedness of principle, see the textbook of the “Online Buddhist Academy of Practicing as Taught,”
A Detailed Explanation of “Notes on Touching the Elephant: Buddha-Recitation Samādhi”
[With neither Chan nor the Pure Land, the iron bed and the brazen post; through ten thousand kalpas, a thousand lives, with no refuge on which to rely at all.]

One who has neither illumined the mind and seen the nature, nor achieved “true faith and earnest vows with single-minded, undisturbed Buddha-recitation,” if at the end of life he cannot keep right mindfulness clear, is dragged along by the power of karma to be reborn in the six paths. Because the delusions of views and thoughts are not cut off, on account of the “three-life enmity” he will revolve for a long time through the three evil destinies, and the time of falling into the hells (the iron bed and the brazen post) is the longest. The Buddha said: Those who obtain a human body are like the soil on a fingernail; those who lose the human body are like the soil of the great earth.

[Three-life enmity] Because of practicing in this life, in the next life one enjoys the reward of blessings, and thereupon, relying on those blessings, one commits evil, which causes one to fall in the life after that. Even when one’s hell-karma is exhausted, one is again reborn as a hungry ghost or an animal; to recover the human body is harder than ever! Hence the World-Honored One, holding up some soil on his hand, asked Ānanda: “Is the soil in my hand more, or the soil of the great earth more?” Ānanda answered: “The soil of the great earth is more.” The Buddha said: “Those who obtain a human body are like the soil in my hand; those who lose the human body are like the soil of the great earth.” Thus “through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lives, with no one to rely upon”! Therefore, if a practitioner does not end birth and death in this life, then after three lives his suffering and evil retribution will be endless—hence the name “three-life enmity.”
Question: To believe, vow, and recite the Buddha’s name while investigating Chan—is that not a muddled mixture, like standing with one foot on each of two boats?

Answer: It is not standing on two boats, but boarding the single boat that can reach the far shore in this very life. The purpose of our studying Buddhism is to become a buddha and deliver living beings. To become a buddha, one must first end the sectioned birth-and-death and escape the cycle, and then end the transformational birth-and-death and realize the fruit of buddhahood. For this present life, the most urgent matter is to end the sectioned birth-and-death and escape the cycle. Those who can cut off the delusions of views and thoughts will certainly escape the cycle of birth and death, and are beyond the scope of our discussion. For those who cannot cut off these delusions, there are three boats: cultivating the Pure Land, cultivating Chan, and cultivating both Chan and Pure Land. Cultivating the Pure Land is the affair of practitioners of the Pure Land school; here we discuss only the two boats of cultivating Chan and of the dual practice.

For one who cultivates Chan alone without cutting off the delusions of views and thoughts, there are two outcomes: “Chan without a Pure Land” and “neither Chan nor a Pure Land.” Since there is no Pure Land, he cannot be born in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, and since the delusions are not cut off, he cannot end birth and death and escape the cycle. In particular, one who cultivates Chan without illumining the mind and seeing the nature (“neither Chan nor a Pure Land”) has an extremely grave outcome—the iron bed and the brazen post. Therefore, for a Chan practitioner who has not cut off the delusions of views and thoughts, there is only one boat by which to end birth and death and escape the cycle: the dual practice of Chan and Pure Land. As to whether the dual practice is a muddled mixture—if it is used well, not only is it not a mixture, but each side enhances the other; try it and you will know for yourself. Consider: if it were a mixture, why would the patriarch Yongming have said, “With both Chan and the Pure Land, like a tiger crowned with horns; in this life a teacher of the people, in the next, a buddha or patriarch born”? The patriarch Yongming himself was one who had come through the dual practice of Chan and Pure Land, and in practice he personally confirmed that the dual practice is mutually enhancing, like a tiger bearing horns—a teacher of the people in this life, a buddha or patriarch in the next.

[Sectioned birth and death] For living beings in the three realms and six paths, through the recompense of good and evil karma, their life spans have their limits and their bodies have their divisions; hence their birth and death is called “sectioned birth and death.” One who ends sectioned birth and death escapes the cycle and leaves the three realms. [Transformational birth and death] The sages of the three vehicles, having cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and ended sectioned birth and death, in the course of their practice have their delusions gradually extinguished and their realization gradually increased. This migration from delusion to realization differs in each phase, and the movement from an earlier phase into a later one is exactly like a birth and death; its transformation is wondrous and unfathomable, beyond conception, and hence is called “transformational birth and death.” One who ends transformational birth and death perfectly realizes the fruit of buddhahood.
Question: Then why cultivate Chan at all?
Answer: Cultivating Chan is suited to the following circumstances:
1. For one who can cut off the delusions of views and thoughts in this very life, or who aims even to transcend the dharmakāya, it is appropriate to cultivate Chan.
2. The distinctive character of Chinese Buddhism lies in Chan; for one who wishes to penetrate Chinese Buddhism and to revitalize it, it is appropriate to cultivate Chan.
3. For one who wishes to become a horn-bearing tiger and broadly deliver living beings, it is appropriate to cultivate Chan.

4. As far as practice is concerned, the Chan school possesses vast, profound theories, methods, and precedents—complete and sudden, sharp and swift. For one whose faculties correspond to Chan and who takes joy in it, it is appropriate to cultivate Chan.
Question: How does one practice Chan and Pure Land together?

Answer: To illumine the mind and see the nature through investigating Chan, there are three stages: 1. The coarse thoughts cease (the ten thousand thoughts return to one); 2. The subtle thoughts cease (the one returns to nothing); 3. The extremely subtle thoughts come to rest and the original nature is thoroughly seen. A Chan practitioner, through investigating Chan, has already achieved “the ten thousand thoughts returning to one,” or “the one returning to nothing,” or even illumined the mind and seen the nature, and so his Buddha-recitation can be single-minded and undisturbed. However, to be born in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, besides single-minded, undisturbed Buddha-recitation, one must also have true faith and earnest vows. Faith is wholehearted trust in the power of the Buddha. In his causal ground, Amitabha Buddha made forty-eight vows, every one of them to deliver living beings; moreover, the Buddha’s power is compassionate and embraces living beings as a mother remembers her child. If, at the end of life, a Chan practitioner can inwardly consolidate right mindfulness, like a child remembering its mother, he is certain to move the Buddha to come and welcome him. Vows are the willingness to be born in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss in this very life, no longer bobbing up and down in this filthy place through many lives and kalpas, passing from delusion into delusion. Moreover, one vows that after being born in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, one will return to this Sahā world to deliver all living beings. Therefore, in the dual practice of Chan and Pure Land, one must apply solid, honest effort to true faith and earnest vows, and achieve single-minded, undisturbed Buddha-recitation, ensuring that at the end of life one earnestly seeks birth in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, consolidating right mindfulness within and eliciting the Buddha’s welcome without. On true faith, earnest vows, and the method of Buddha-recitation, see the academy’s textbook
Aware Buddha-Recitation
If one uses investigative Buddha-recitation for the dual practice of Chan and Pure Land, it is even more direct. For the method of investigative Buddha-recitation, see
Investigative Buddha-Recitation

[Coarse thoughts, subtle thoughts, and extremely subtle thoughts] For example, for one who recites the Buddha’s name, the deluded thoughts are the coarse thoughts, and the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name is the subtle thought. Usually, when both the coarse and the subtle thoughts have ceased, this is called “no-thought”—the commonly spoken-of no-thought. Further, if the extremely subtle thought also ceases, that is the ultimate no-thought. [Extremely subtle thought] The extremely subtle arising and ceasing, the flowing transformation, of the discriminating mind; it is the aspect of the ālaya-consciousness.
Question: What are the similarities and differences between Chan and Pure Land?

Answer: As far as practice is concerned, whatever the Dharma gate, the path is the same: the ten thousand thoughts return to one, the one returns to nothing, the mind is illumined and the nature seen, the delusions of views and thoughts are cut off, the forbearance of non-arising is attained, and the fruit of buddhahood is perfectly realized.

The Pure Land school recites Amitabha Buddha of the Western Land of Utmost Bliss and seeks birth in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. As long as, through Buddha-recitation, one achieves “the ten thousand thoughts returning to one” (single-mindedness without distraction), one is certain to be born in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss at the end of life. When the flower opens and one sees the Buddha, one immediately attains the forbearance of non-arising (when the flower opens and one sees the Buddha, one awakens to non-arising), and then perfectly realizes the fruit of buddhahood. If, after achieving single-minded, undisturbed Buddha-recitation, one wishes to raise the grade of one’s rebirth, one may go further and cultivate the Buddha-recitation samādhi, whereby “the one returns to nothing” and the mind is illumined and the nature seen (on the Buddha-recitation samādhi, see the textbook of the “Online Buddhist Academy of Practicing as Taught,”
A Detailed Explanation of “Notes on Touching the Elephant: Buddha-Recitation Samādhi”
). Of course, one may continue further, cut off the delusions of views and thoughts, and then attain the forbearance of non-arising.

Investigating Chan is through looking into the huatou: the ten thousand thoughts return to one (single-mindedness without distraction), the one returns to nothing (not a single thought arises), and the mind is illumined and the nature seen; then, through preserving and sustaining the realization while eliminating residual habits, one cuts off the delusions of views and thoughts, and only then can one end birth and death.

Contemplating the mind is through observing the stream of consciousness manifesting karma in one’s own mind: not a single thought arises, the mind is illumined and the nature seen; then, through preserving and sustaining the realization while eliminating residual habits, one cuts off the delusions of views and thoughts, and only then can one end birth and death.

Therefore, the two great Dharma gates of the Chan school—investigating Chan and contemplating the mind—both require cutting off the delusions of views and thoughts before birth and death can be ended. But in the Pure Land school, with faith and vows and upholding the Name, one need only have
ten continuous recitations at the time of death

to respond and connect with the Buddha, moving Amitabha Buddha to come and lead one on, and thereby, relying on the Buddha’s power, one is born in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, ending birth and death and escaping the cycle. Hence the
Pure Rules of the Chan monastery first set down by Chan Master Baizhang
(the “Essential Principles of the Monastery”) begin by saying:
“A monastery flourishes when it is free of affairs,
practice is most secure when it rests on Buddha-recitation
On “ten continuous recitations at the time of death, and birth is attained,” see
How Can One Attain Rebirth

Question: The Fourth Patriarch of the Chan school, Master Daoxin, said: “Objects and conditions have no good or ill; good and ill arise within the mind. If the mind does not forcibly name them, whence could deluded feelings arise? When deluded feelings do not arise, the true mind freely knows all. Only follow the mind in freedom, with no more remedial contrivance—this is called the ever-abiding dharmakāya, without change.” This instruction is the most direct method of practice; why must one go through “the ten thousand thoughts return to one, the one returns to nothing, illumine the mind and see the nature,” and so on?
Answer: This instruction of the Fourth Patriarch was given to Chan Master Farong of Mount Niutou (see
The Fourth Patriarch’s Instructions to Farong

). At that time, Farong had already cultivated to the point that “a hundred birds brought flowers in their beaks (to offer him),” a marvel, and moreover, “the Fourth Patriarch, observing the signs from afar, knew that on that mountain (Mount Niutou) there was an extraordinary person, and so he personally went to seek him out.” Hence the Fourth Patriarch said to him:
“To cut off thought and deliberation—this Dharma you have now already attained.”
(This means: the work of safeguarding has already been accomplished by you.) Then he gave the targeted instruction on how to do the work of spontaneous following:
“Only follow the mind in freedom, with no more remedial contrivance.”

But for ordinary people, if when facing situations and meeting conditions one cannot manage “the mind does not forcibly name them,” then one should first do the work of safeguarding, beginning from “the ten thousand thoughts return to one.” In fact, before Farong met the Fourth Patriarch, he too began his cultivation from “the ten thousand thoughts return to one”—or in a previous life he had begun from there.
